chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 411 to 420, Peyanar's mullai decade of the hero praising the season (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து): home again as the rains begin, the hero invites his wife to bathe and play in the flowering scrub, likens the peacocks and the beasts to the two of them, calls youth sweet when spent together, wonders whether she is a woman of the sky, and promises the scrub itself that they will come to see it.

411.reading: The hero tells his wife that the full-voiced cloud has scattered its heavy drops and the rains have begun in the lovely scrub, and bids her, the woman of long dark hair, come quickly so they may bathe together in the new water that is falling.
411.nuance: The first rain that once marked the deadline of his absence is now an invitation to play: the season the waiting wife dreaded is turned, by his return, into a holiday for both.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains beginning in the scrub

comparisons.tenor: the scrub in flower, as a woman adorned

412.reading: The hero tells his wife that with kaayaa, konrai, water lily and mullai, the thalavam opening its buds and the pidavam in bloom, the scrub has grown lovely and put on an ornament of flowers, and asks her, the woman of large wide eyes, to come quickly and play there.
412.nuance: The catalogue is of mullai's own rain flowers; the scrub is pictured as a woman who has dressed herself (பூவணி கொண்டன்று), the adornment he once could not give his wife while away. The நெய்தல் here is the lily of the scrub's pools, not a token of the seashore.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowers of the rainy scrub

thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து) names the hero, home again, praising the rainy season

413.reading: The hero tells his wife that in the cool scrub, fragrant as her own brow, the peacocks dance just as she does and the season of rain has begun, a time for the two of them to delight in.
413.nuance: The comparison runs backwards: the woman is the standard and the peacock is likened to her (நின்னே போல), and the scrub smells of her brow rather than she of it; the land is read through her.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool scrub as the rains begin

414.reading: The hero bids his gentle wife look at the scrub grown rich and fragrant, where birds and beasts frisk happily in pairs and many flowers have come to fullness on the trees and creepers.
414.nuance: Birds and beasts together, not one pair, so the pairing is the season's general mood rather than an image of the couple; a reader may still feel it as the land joining in their reunion.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து) names the hero, home again, praising the rainy season

415.reading: The hero tells the young woman that this is the season they longed for and that the scrub they kept in mind; youth is sweet if spent together, and sweet indeed now is the union.
415.nuance: The near and far demonstratives (இதுவே, உதுவே) point at the time and the place as if both had been promised; the season they 'longed for' is the one that ended his absence. Line 4's அவர்ப் புணர்வு, 'union with them', shifts to the third person and is hard to fit to a speech addressed to மடந்தை.

thinai_evidence.note: the season and the scrub they had looked forward to

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து) names the hero, home again, praising the rainy season; line 4 turns to the third person (அவர்), so the addressee may change

comparisons.tenor: the hero who has embraced the girl

416.reading: As the tusker has embraced his young she-elephant in the lovely bush where bees, drunk on pollen from the fragrant blossom dust of the scrub, hum loudly, so we have embraced the girl of shining bangles, says the hero.
416.nuance: The two closing words answer each other, மாவே and யாமே: the hero sets his own embrace beside the elephant's without a marker, so the beasts are a stated parallel, not a hidden one.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து) names the hero, home again, praising the rainy season; he speaks of the girl in the third person, to no one named

417.reading: The rains have mingled with the scrub and the fields have spread out level with many crops together; and as the pollen-laden bees swarmed in beauty, the woman of flower-filled hair embraced me, says the hero.
417.nuance: ஏர் in line 2 can be beauty or the plough; with the fields spread level it may be the ploughing of the first rains, which would set the couple's embrace beside the farmers' sowing.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains come to the scrub

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து) names the hero, home again, praising the rainy season; he speaks of her in the third person (முயங்கினள்), to no one named

418.reading: In the scrub made lovely to see, where the rain-bird's drought has been ended and the heavy drops have poured without stopping, the hero asks his wife whether she is a woman of the sky, she who held him close against her fine breasts.
418.nuance: வானம் பாடி can be the rain-calling bird whose thirst is ended, or the sky that 'sang' (thundered) and drove off the drought; the line division decides it. The hero's question makes the embrace of his own wife a wonder, as if no earthly woman could give it.

419.reading: The hero bids the young woman look at the beasts of the scrub: like the two of them, whose faultless bond has mingled their lives into one, the beasts embrace in a fresh union that knows no parting and have joined delightfully.
419.nuance: Again the humans are the standard (நம்போல்): the couple's bond is what the beasts are measured against. பிரிந்துறல் அறியா, 'not knowing parting', is said of the beasts but speaks for a couple who have just come through a parting.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து) names the hero, home again, praising the rainy season

420.reading: The hero tells the scrub that it has come to fine beauty, with konrai blooming like gold, honeyed kaayaa like sapphire, and the thondri in flower, and that he will come to see it with his bright-browed woman, drawn by its choice loveliness.
420.nuance: The decade closes with the land addressed as a host: the season he praised all through is now a place he promises to visit with her, not a deadline he must beat.

links.note: Kuruntokai's waiting woman says the men went for wealth without regard for youth (இளமை பாரார்); Ainkurunuru's returned hero says youth is sweet if spent together (இனிதுடன் கழிக்கின் இளமை).
links.teaches: The charge the abandoned woman makes in the rains is answered in the same season by the man come home, who adopts her measure of youth as his own, so the two poems stage the mullai argument over youth and wealth from both sides of the parting.

links.note: The Naladiyar says the passing joy of youth is not found among the wise; the Ainkurunuru hero says youth spent together is sweet and the union is sweet now.
links.teaches: Both accept that youth passes, but the Naladiyar draws from that fact a duty to withhold delight, while the Sangam hero draws from it a reason to spend youth in shared pleasure, so the same premise yields opposite counsel in the old love poetry and the later ascetic quatrains.

links.note: In Kuruntokai the stag frisking with its sweet mate in the cool rain seems to taunt the waiting woman; in Ainkurunuru the hero shows his wife the beasts joined in delight, like us.
links.teaches: The paired beasts of the rainy scrub are one image read two ways: before the return they reproach the absent man through the woman's grief, after it they mirror the couple's reunion, so the image takes its sense from whether the speaker is still waiting.

links.note: The Kural's man says the bond between him and the girl is like that of body and life; the Ainkurunuru hero speaks of their faultless bond as lives mingled into one (உயிர்கலந்து ஒன்றிய).
links.teaches: The Kural states the life-bond as a lover's private claim, while the Ainkurunuru hero, past a parting, finds it acted out by the scrub's mating beasts and makes the couple the measure of them, so the general likeness gains a witness in the season of return.

links.note: In Akananuru 134 the returning hero hushes his chariot so the stag and doe in union are not parted; in Ainkurunuru 414, now home, he bids his wife look at birds and beasts frisking in pairs.
links.teaches: On the road the hero shields the beasts' union as a sign of the one he is hurrying to, and once home he shows the paired creatures to his wife as a shared sight, so the mullai beasts move from his private token to the couple's common pleasure.

links.note: Both use the same pair of similes for the rain flowers: konrai like gold (பொன் என), kaayaa like sapphire (மணி என); Natrinai's returning hero urges his charioteer on, Ainkurunuru's promises to bring his wife to see the scrub.
links.teaches: The same jewelled konrai and kaayaa that make the returning man in Natrinai hurry home become, once he is home, a sight he promises to return to with his wife, so the formula's force changes from summons to leisure with the man's place in the journey.

links.note: Natrinai's hero, back from his work, blesses the cloud whose night rain fell on the town where he lay embraced with his wife; Ainkurunuru's says the rains mingled with the scrub and she embraced him.
links.teaches: Natrinai turns the coincidence of rain and embrace into thanks owed to the cloud, while Ainkurunuru sets the two side by side without comment, so together they show the returning hero crediting the season with the reunion it once threatened.

links.note: The Kural's man says an embrace no breeze can part is sweet to two who love; the Ainkurunuru hero asks if his wife, who held him close against her breasts (மாண்முலை அடைய முயங்கியோயே), is a woman of the sky.
links.teaches: The Kural names the close embrace as a pleasure common to all lovers, but the Ainkurunuru hero, after absence, finds the same embrace so beyond the human that he takes his own wife for a celestial, so the general sweetness is shown as wonder when it is regained.

source_issues: The decade's colophon gives no thurai for any poem; the speaker and situation are taken from the decade title கிழவன் பருவம் பாராட்டுப் பத்து.
415 line 4: அவர்ப் புணர்வே puts the beloved in the third person in a poem addressed to மடந்தை; the reading is marked uncertain.
418 line 1: வானம் பாடி is printed as two words and may be the rain-bird வானம்பாடி or the sky singing; marked uncertain.
413 line 4: நாநயத்தகவே is printed run together, apparently நாம் நயத்தகவே.
420 line 1: பொன்னெனமலர்ந்த is printed without word breaks (பொன் என மலர்ந்த).
